security_spec.violation_condition: In a future FreeBSD RISC-V bhype IOMMU driver, when software sets DC.iohgatp.MODE to Bare (disabling second-stage address translation because the guest runs with direct physical access or identity mapping) but leaves DC.msiptp.MODE != Off, the IOMMU will attempt MSI page-table walks with no valid GSCID context, causing MSI translations to be resolved in an undefined or stale VM address space
security_spec.summary: When iohgatp.MODE is Bare (no second-stage translation), msiptp.MODE must be Off; failing to enforce this in bhyve's DDT/DC programming allows a guest VM's MSI interrupts to be routed through stale or host-owned GSCID context, enabling VM escape via MSI interrupt redirection

findings.finding: RISC-V bhyve vmmops_gla2gpa is a stub returning ENOSYS — there is no IOMMU driver for RISC-V bhyve at all. When a future RISC-V IOMMU driver is written, the developer must ensure DC.iohgatp.MODE=Bare and DC.msiptp.MODE!=Off are mutually exclusive, or MSI page-table walks will resolve in an undefined VM address space with no valid GSCID context. This stub is the primary injection point where the vulnerability would manifest.

iommu_init() only handles Intel (iommu_ops_intel) and AMD (iommu_ops_amd) — there is no RISC-V path. When a RISC-V iommu_ops backend is added, the new code must validate that when DC.iohgatp.MODE is Bare (identity-map passthrough), DC.msiptp.MODE must also be Off, otherwise MSI translations resolve in a stale or unspecified GSCID address space. The x86 VT-d path in vtd.c uses DOMID-based context entries that don't have this split-mode hazard; RISC-V's DDT-based device_context table introduces a new class of inconsistency bug not present on x86.

vmmops_run writes hgatp via csr_write(hgatp, pmap->pm_satp) at line 630, setting up second-stage guest physical translation. The RISC-V H-extension uses hgatp for CPU-side stage-2 translation. A future RISC-V IOMMU driver would separately manage DC.iohgatp (the IOMMU's analogue of hgatp in the device-context table) and DC.msiptp. If the IOMMU driver replicates the vmmops_run pattern of independently setting iohgatp without checking msiptp consistency, the vulnerability triggers: DC.iohgatp.MODE=Bare (passthrough/identity) while DC.msiptp.MODE=Sv39x4/Sv48x4 would cause MSI walks to reference a stale or non-existent GSCID. The hfence_gvma at line 628 only fences CPU TLB, not IOMMU TLB.

The IOMMU_DOMAIN_IDMAP flag at line 147 shows the framework already understands identity-mapped domains (where DC.iohgatp.MODE would logically be Bare). In an x86 context this flag is safe because VT-d context entries don't have an independent MSI-PT mode — the translation enable affects all request types uniformly. However, a RISC-V IOMMU driver that maps this flag to DC.iohgatp.MODE=Bare must additionally enforce DC.msiptp.MODE=Off. The flag itself is correctly defined; the compliance gap is that no RISC-V IOMMU driver exists to misuse it.
findings.snippet:
#define	IOMMU_DOMAIN_GAS_INITED		0x0001
#define	IOMMU_DOMAIN_PGTBL_INITED	0x0002
#define	IOMMU_DOMAIN_IDMAP		0x0010	/* Domain uses identity
						   page table */
#define	IOMMU_DOMAIN_RMRR		0x0020	/* Domain contains RMRR entry,
						   cannot be turned off */

findings.finding: The host domain is created with a 1:1 identity mapping from 0 to maxaddr. On x86 VT-d/AMD-Vi, there is no split between first-stage (GVA→GPA) and second-stage (GPA→HPA) translation for MSIs in the IOMMU — MSI address regions are either within the identity-mapped window or handled via interrupt remapping tables. This is architecturally safe on x86 because VT-d context entries don't have an independent 'MSI page-table pointer' like RISC-V's DC.msiptp. The spec hazard is RISC-V-specific.
